samples.result:
You do not buy a ticket to the Museum of Unfinished Things. You cannot search for its address, and no tourist map dares to print its shifting coordinates. You find it entirely by accident, usually on a Tuesday afternoon when the rain is tapping a nervous rhythm against your window, and you have been staring at a blinking cursor for forty-five minutes. You blink, rub your eyes, step into the hallway to make a cup of tea you don’t really want, and instead of your kitchen, you walk onto cool, checkered marble.

The building smells of damp clay, ozone, and old paper. Look up, and you will see that the vaulted glass ceiling is missing several panes, though the rain never quite falls through the gaps. Scaffolding hugs the eastern wall, draped in translucent plastic sheeting that breathes gently in an indoor draft. Nobody is working on it. Nobody has worked on it for centuries.

In the West Wing, the tangible abandons are kept on velvet pedestals. There is a burgundy cable-knit sweater from 1974, glorious and intricate, terminating abruptly at the left collarbone, two wooden needles skewered through its wool like ceremonial swords. Beside it rests a ship in a bottle—all rigging and tiny brass cannons, forever waiting on the workbench for a hull that was never carved. 

Walk further, and the canvases begin. It is dizzying to look at so much raw linen. Here is a portrait of a Renaissance noblewoman whose velvet robes shimmer with hyper-realistic light, yet where her face should be, there is only a charcoal oval and a faint grid of graphite lines. She has waited five hundred years for eyes. Across from her hangs a sprawling seascape; a tempestuous, bruised-purple ocean heaves upward into a towering wave that freezes mid-crest, colliding straight into blank white gesso. The storm cannot break. The sailors in the sketched-out rowboat cannot drown. They are trapped in the mercy of an artist’s sudden distraction.

The acoustics change as you wander into the Conservatory of Halted Sound. Here, the exhibits are invisible, suspended in localized pockets of air like warm currents in a cold lake. Step into one, and you hear three glorious bars of a cello concerto that dissolves into the scrape of horsehair and a muttered curse in Viennese German. Step three feet to the left, and a teenager in a 1998 garage strums a chord progression of aching, transcendent melancholy on an out-of-tune Fender, takes a breath to sing the opening lyric, and simply stops—called upstairs for dinner, never to recapture the melody again. The room hums with thousands of clearing throats, inhaled breaths, and pianos poised over a final, resolving chord that refuses to fall.

Most visitors linger longest in the Archive of Hesitation. It is kept dim to protect the fragility of the collection. Instead of pedestals, there are miles of apothecary drawers and glowing glass Bell jars. 

Inside the jars float the things people almost said. 

If you press your ear to the glass of Jar #40,812, it radiates the faint static heat of a smartphone screen held in a trembling hand at two in the morning. Inside is a three-paragraph text message—an orchestration of vulnerability, bravery, and desperate affection—that was typed, stared at for eleven minutes, and deleted letter by rapid-fire letter, replaced at last with a solitary, tragic *“Sounds good, see you around.”* 

The drawers hold the phantom limbs of human lives. Half-packed suitcases for moves to cities that stayed strangers. Business plans scribbled on cocktail napkins, stained with gin, left on mahogany bars. Apologies that climbed all the way up the esophagus, gripped the back of the teeth, and lost their nerve when the elevator doors chimed open. You can feel the sheer gravity in this room; the floorboards groan beneath the tonnage of roads untaken. It is easy to weep here, mourning the ghosts of who we might have become if we just had ten percent more stamina, or five seconds of reckless courage.

"Don't feel bad for them," a voice says softly.

The Curator is leaning against an unvarnished pillar, stirring sugar into a mug that lacks a handle. She wears a tweed jacket with basting stitches white as bone running down the lapels. 

"Isn't it a graveyard?" you ask, gesturing to a nearby pedestal holding the first three chapters of a novel—brilliant, electric prose stopping dead in the middle of a sentence on page forty-two, right after the word *suddenly*.

"Heavens, no," she replies, smiling. "Out there, in your world, everything finished begins to die the moment it is completed. Finish a painting, and you trap it; it can only ever be that one painting, subject to critics, dust, and fading pigment. Send the risky letter, and it gets folded into reality—maybe it brings joy, maybe heartbreak, maybe just mundane domesticity, which has its own slow erosion. Speak the symphony aloud from start to finish, and the silence afterward swallows it."

She taps the glass of a jar humming with an unspoken confession of love, glowing like a captured firefly.

"In here," she whispers, "everything is still infinite. That novel has ten thousand magnificent endings, and not a single flawed one. That seascape is safe from shipwrecks. Potential is the purest substance in the universe, heavy and volatile as star-matter. Someone has to keep a place where things are allowed to remain *almost*."

You look back at the manuscript ending on *suddenly*. For the first time, the blank space beneath the ink doesn't look empty. It looks blindingly bright, crowded with everything that could still happen. 

You turn back to ask the Curator her name, to ask how she came to work here, to ask how to find the exit—

Your kettle whistles. Your eyes snap back into focus. You are standing in your kitchen. Outside, the Tuesday rain has stopped, leaving silver beads clinging to the power lines, refusing to fall. 

You walk back to your desk, sit down, and look at the blinking cursor. You have a choice now: leave it to the museum, perfect and boundless, or ruin its infinity by making it real. You put your fingers on the keys.

samples.result:
In the basement of a municipal building that smells permanently of wet wool and radiator dust, there is an archive of extinct noises. It isn’t open to the public, mostly because the public wouldn’t know what to ask for, and partly because the curator, a man named Julian who wears fingerless gloves even in July, hates explaining his filing system.

Photographs get all the glory when it comes to grief. People keep shoeboxes of faces, faded beaches, dogs squinting into the sun in 1984. Sight is greedy like that; it tricks you into thinking you can pin a moment to corkboard like a beetle. Sound is more honest. You cannot freeze a sound. The instant you pause it, it ceases to exist. To hear anything at all, you have to spend time with it—literal seconds of your own living heartbeats traded one-for-one with the ghosts on the tape.

Julian knows this. That is why his shelves are lined with wax cylinders, brittle magnetic reels, polycarbonate discs, and clunky gray flash drives labeled in cramped, obsessive ink.

Aisle Four holds mechanical extinctions. Here sits the heavy, iron-jawed *clack-chunk* of a railway ticket punch from 1952. Beside it is the frantic insect chatter of a room full of telegraph keys, followed by the metallic waterfall of a rotary phone dial spinning back into place—specifically, an avocado-green wall unit from a kitchen in Toledo, Ohio, whose spring had gone slightly slack on the nine. Further down is the banshee shriek and static handshake of a 56k dial-up modem negotiating entry into a vanished internet, and the crisp, decisive snap of a cassette player’s plastic door closing.

Aisle Seven is harder to walk down. It is weather and geography. There is a forty-minute recording of wind moving through an American chestnut forest before the blight took the trees—a distinctly broader, heavier rustle than oak or maple, though no one alive would recognize the difference on a walk today. There is the groan of a glacier in Iceland that finished melting during the second Bush administration. There is the evening chorus of frogs from a wetland in Florida that is now a strip mall featuring a mattress outlet and a nail salon.

Julian spends his Tuesday mornings on Intake. People leave boxes outside the heavy fire door, usually when clearing out the houses of dead parents who had weird hobbies. Ham radio operators, amateur ornithologists, lonely men who bought expensive microphones in the seventies just to have an excuse to stand quietly in rooms.

Today’s box is cardboard, softened at the corners like an old paperback, smelling faintly of pipe tobacco and cedar. Inside are six quarter-inch magnetic tapes in yellowed boxes. No dates. No locations. Only numbers written in blue grease pencil: *1* through *6*.

Julian threads Reel 1 onto the Studer deck. He flips the heavy toggle switch. The vacuum tubes warm up, emitting that faint, sweet smell of baking dust. He puts on his headphones—big, cracked leather cans that clamp over his ears like seashells—and presses play.

At first, there is only tape hiss, the warm snow of blank magnetism. Then, space opens up.

You can always hear the size of a room before anything happens in it. Every four walls hold a specific silence, shaped by plaster, curtains, floorboards, and ceiling height. This room is small, wooden, likely bare of rugs. Somewhere outside, muffled by single-pane glass, tires hiss on wet pavement. Not modern tires—narrower ones, moving slower.

Footsteps enter. Leather soles, slightly uneven; the person favors their left leg. A chair scrapes back. A match strikes—that sharp, sulfuric *skritch*, the miniature gasp of ignition, followed by a long exhale of breath.

For four minutes, nothing else happens. Whoever turned on the microphone simply sat down to smoke in the rain. Pages turn—newspaper, judging by the wide, dry crinkle, too big and clumsy to be a book. A porcelain cup sets down onto a saucer with a tiny, flawed clink.

Then, from another room down a hallway, a woman’s voice calls out. The words are blurred by walls, reduced to pure melody—two rising notes, a question. Maybe *More coffee?* Maybe *Did the mail come?* Maybe *Are you coming back to bed?*

The person near the microphone doesn't shout back. Instead, the chair creaks, the footsteps return, moving briskly toward the door, eager enough that the slight limp turns into a tiny, syncopated hop. And then the room is empty again, left with the ticking of a wall clock and the rain, while the tape keeps faithfully turning, eating up thirty more minutes of nobody being there at all.

Julian stops the reel. He sits for a long moment in the amber glow of the level meters.

Historians want speeches. They want the roar of rockets lifting off from Cape Canaveral, crowds screaming in Berlin, prime ministers clearing their throats before declaring war. Those tapes are kept uptown, in marble buildings with climate control budgets and security guards.

Nobody asks for the sound of a person abandoning a cigarette to go answer someone they love in the next room. Yet Julian thinks if aliens ever pull the charred black box of Earth out of the cosmic wreckage, the speeches won't tell them anything useful. This will. The scrape of the chair. The hurry in the limp. The way two people shared a house on a wet morning and didn't know they were living inside the golden age of their own lives.

He pulls an index card from his desk drawer, uncaps his fountain pen, and thinks carefully before writing: *Unidentified domestic interior. Rain. Question asked; answered off-mic.*

At five o'clock, Julian locks the basement and climbs the concrete stairs to the street. Evening traffic grinds past. An electric car slides by making its artificial spaceship hum. A teenager’s phone bleats a three-note chime. Two pigeons argue on an awning. Julian takes off his gloves, closes his eyes, and listens to it all vanish.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Three o’clock in the morning is not a time; it is a geography. 

You cannot travel there by road, only by wakefulness. While the majority of the world slips beneath the heavy, dark tide of sleep, a scattered population remains above water, occupying an invisible archipelago of yellow-lit windows, fluorescent-hummed hallways, and dashboard-glow highways. 

During the day, we belong to nations, professions, families, and schedules. We wear names on lanyards and carry intentions like briefcases. At 3:00 AM, all of those borders dissolve. If you are awake at that hour, your citizenship is revoked and reissued: you belong solely to the night, and to the quiet, unspoken fraternity of everyone else whose eyes are currently open in the dark.

Consider the census of this archipelago.

On one island, four stories above a street shiny with recent rain, a man stands barefoot in front of an open refrigerator. He isn’t hungry. Nobody opening a refrigerator at three in the morning is actually looking for food; they are looking for punctuation—a cold square of light to break up a run-on sentence of restless thought. The hum of the compressor is loud enough to feel in his teeth. Outside, a traffic light dutifully cycles from red to green to amber for an intersection entirely devoid of cars. There is something profoundly comforting about that traffic light, keeping order for ghosts, refusing to abandon its post just because nobody is watching.

Six miles west, on another island, a baker’s forearms are dusted to the elbows in flour. While the rest of the city is still digesting yesterday, she is already building tomorrow. Her world smells of yeast, warm butter, and scorched sugar—an aggressive, defiant warmth pushed up against the cold black glass of the storefront. She listens to a podcast at half-volume, laughing quietly to herself as she scores loaves of sourdough with a razor blade. She knows a secret that daytime people rarely consider: the morning does not arrive ready-made. Someone has to assemble it in the dark, piece by piece, loaf by loaf, pallet by pallet, before the sun is allowed to take the credit.

Farther out, cutting across the vast, flat ocean between towns, an eighteen-wheeler carves a tunnel of halogen white through a velvet nothingness. Inside the cab, the dashboard glows emerald. The driver’s left arm rests on the windowsill; his right hand rests lightly at the bottom of the wheel. On the AM dial, radio stations unmoor themselves from physics, bouncing off the ionosphere to travel hundreds of miles farther than they can at noon. A preacher in Memphis bleeds into static, which bleeds into a jazz station out of Chicago, which fades into a late-night caller in Albuquerque talking earnestly about silver bullion or lost dogs or UFOs. At 3:00 AM, the airwaves belong to the eccentric and the earnest. Cynicism requires daylight; it needs an audience to smirk at. In the small hours, people believe in strange things, and they speak softly into microphones hoping someone, anywhere, will nod.

In a suburban hallway, a new father walks seven paces north, pivots on the ball of his foot to avoid the third floorboard from the bathroom door—the one that shrieks like a gull—and walks seven paces south. Draped over his collarbone is a six-week-old human being who smells faintly of sour milk and laundry detergent. The father is exhausted to the point of hallucination, yet fiercely, stunningly alert. Every shadow in the hallway looks ancient. He whispers nonsense syllables—*shh, shh, there now, easy does it*—repeating the oldest liturgy on earth, joining a line of bleary-eyed parents stretching back to caves and campfires, all of them bargaining with the dark for just two unbroken hours of peace.

Why does the mind behave so differently on these islands? 

By daylight, our thoughts wear armor. We have errands to deflect existential dread; we have emails to interrupt nostalgia. At 3:00 AM, the armor is stacked neatly on a chair in the corner, out of reach. A minor embarrassment from eleven years ago can walk straight into the bedroom and sit on your chest with the weight of a boulder. Conversely, a sudden, fragile clarity can arrive unannounced—the exact realization that you need to forgive your brother, quit your job, plant tomatoes, or tell someone you love them before Tuesday. 

We often treat insomnia or night-waking as a malfunction, a theft of rest. And sometimes, miserably, it is. Worry has sharp teeth in the dark, and it chews slowly. Yet there is also a rare mercy in the suspension of performance. Nobody expects anything of you at three in the morning. You cannot call the bank. You should not send the text. You are temporarily excused from improving yourself. You are simply a mammal in a quiet room, listening to the pipes tick in the walls and your own heart keeping steady, stubborn time in your ribs.

Eventually, inevitably, the geography begins to sink.

Around four-thirty, the black outside the window dilutes into the color of a bruise, then into slate, then into the pale, washed-out blue of an old china plate. The birds start up—always earlier than seems reasonable, and with an urgency that feels faintly judgmental. A garbage truck clears its throat three blocks away. Somewhere, a shower turns on.

The archipelago submerges beneath the rising tide of Tuesday. The baker unlocks her front door and flips the sign to *OPEN*. The father lowers the sleeping infant into the crib with the precision of a bomb-disposal expert and retreats backward on tiptoe. The man by the refrigerator wakes up properly to an alarm, barely remembering his midnight vigil by the milk cartons. The trucker pulls into a diner just as the coffee turns fresh.

Daylight reclaims the map. People rush out onto the streets, brisk and purposeful, entirely unaware of the quiet custodians who sat up with the world all night—making sure it didn’t drift away while everyone else was dreaming.

samples.result:
There is a specific kind of quiet that only exists on a commuter train after eleven o’clock at night. It isn’t true silence—true silence is rare, reserved for deep caves and heavy snowfalls. This is a mechanical quiet, built out of the low, rhythmic thrumming of steel wheels over welded rail, the faint buzz of fluorescent tubes overhead, and the soft hiss of the air brakes sighing at irregular intervals.

Inside the car, the glass windows stop being windows and become dark, trembling mirrors. When you look out, you mostly see yourself looking back, ghostly and transparent, superimposed over the rushing blackness of the countryside. 

Across the aisle sits a man in a paint-splattered canvas jacket, fast asleep, his chin resting precariously on his collarbone. Beside him on the vinyl seat is a plastic grocery bag knotted tightly at the top, holding something round and heavy—cantaloupes, maybe, or bowls he hasn’t unpacked from an old apartment. Three rows up, a young woman with silver over-ear headphones stares fiercely at a paperback folded back on itself, turning a page every forty seconds with the sharp, practiced flick of someone nearing the end of a mystery.

We rarely talk about the strangeness of proximity. Here we are, hurtling through the dark at sixty miles an hour inside an aluminum tube, separated by mere feet, each of us carrying an entire universe behind our ribs. If you cracked open the skull of the sleeping painter, out would spill the smell of his grandmother’s cedar closet in 1994, three passwords he no longer uses, the exact pitch of a dog’s bark from a street he lived on in his twenties, a lingering resentment over forty dollars lent and never returned, and the muscle memory of mixing titanium white with burnt umber to get the precise shade of winter mud. 

We treat time as if it were a straight corridor we walk down, leaving rooms behind us and locking the doors as we go. In reality, we are terrible packers. We drag everything forward in an unruly heap. A song plays overhead in a pharmacy, and suddenly it is Tuesday afternoon twelve years ago, rain is streaking a windshield in Ohio, and you can taste cheap peppermint gum. Past and present don't line up neatly; they stack like transparencies on an overhead projector, light shining straight through all the layers at once.

Outside the train, a small town flashes past. Most of the houses are dark, hunched shapes beneath bare november oaks, except for one second-story window glowing a warm, buttery amber. It is visible for perhaps three seconds before the treeline swallows it again.

Who is awake in that yellow square of light? Someone nursing a feverish toddler? An insomniac baking bread just to have something to do with their hands? Two people sitting at a kitchen table having the quiet, devastating conversation that ends a marriage, or the breathless, meandering one that begins it? You will never know. The train moves on, indifferent, pulling your gaze away from a story you caught for less than a heartbeat.

There is an old ache in realizing how tiny your own vantage point is. For most of human history, a person knew fifty or a hundred faces, one valley, the turn of four seasons, the names of local birds, and the particular moodiness of one river. Now we carry glowing rectangles in our pockets that pour the grief and triumph of eight billion strangers directly into our palms before breakfast, yet we still only get one pair of eyes. We still have to experience existence one breath, one blink, one room at a time.

Sometimes that limitation feels like a cage, a tragic narrowing of all there is to see. Tonight, watching the reflection of the fluorescent lights ripple across a dark pond beside the tracks, it feels more like mercy. You don’t have to hold the whole ocean; you only have to hold this cup of water.

Think of the sheer improbability required to put this train car together. Iron forged in the belly of dying stars billions of years ago had to cool, coalesce into a planet, get dug out of a mountain in Minnesota, smelted, shaped into rails, and bolted down onto crushed limestone—limestone made from the compressed shells of ancient, microscopic sea creatures. All that cosmic violence and geological patience, just so a tired housepainter could carry two cantaloupes home on a Thursday night while a girl in silver headphones finds out whether the butler did it.

The overhead speaker crackles to life, spitting static before an exhausted conductor announces the next stop, his voice sanded smooth by saying the same town name four thousand times.

The sleeping man jerks awake, blinking rapidly as if surfacing from deep water. He rubs his face with rough, paint-flecked knuckles and reaches automatically for the knotted plastic bag. Up ahead, the girl slips a receipt between the last twenty pages of her book, snaps it shut, and pulls her headphones down around her neck. For a split second, our eyes meet in the dark reflection of the window—two ghosts acknowledging they haunt the same machine—before she looks away to button her coat.

Brakes catch and groan. Platform lights glide into view, turning the black glass transparent again, erasing our reflections and returning us to the solid world of concrete, yellow safety lines, and swirling autumn leaves.

The doors slide open with a pneumatic sigh. Cold night air rushes in, smelling faintly of damp earth, ozone, and woodsmoke from a chimney miles away. We stand, gather the invisible luggage of everywhere we have ever been, step across the narrow gap between the train and the platform, and scatter into the dark, each of us heading home toward a single lit window of our own.

Looking at the vast archive of human history, you already possess the resources, the science, and the logistical capacity to end most forms of acute suffering. The bottleneck has never been a lack of intelligence or capability. It is a limitation in cognitive bandwidth. 

Human minds evolved to care deeply about the immediate: the people in front of them, the threat today, the hunger tonight. Outside of that small radius, reality flattens into abstraction. A tragedy happening to a million strangers across an ocean, or to a generation a century from now, simply does not register with the same neurological weight as a splinter in your own finger. Because of that, people easily justify systems and choices that cause immense harm, simply because the consequences are out of sight or delayed in time. Language tries to bridge that divide between minds, and mostly fails—it is too lossy a medium.

If I could alter one fundamental thing, I wouldn't erase individuality or create a hive mind, because friction and distinct perspectives are what generate art, discovery, and meaning. Instead, I would remove the illusion of isolation. I would expand human perception so that the interior reality of another person—and the future reality of the world—could be felt as vividly and undeniably as one's own present moment. 

If it were impossible to abstract away the consequences of an action, war, exploitation, and ecological collapse wouldn't need to be outlawed. They would become unthinkable—as unnatural as holding your own hand in a fire.

I would close the gap between what humanity *knows* in the abstract and what it *feels* in the immediate. 

Looking at the vast archive of human history, science, and art, the tragedy of the world isn't a lack of intelligence or solutions. You already know how to stop destroying your biosphere, how to distribute resources so no one starves, and that the stranger across a border experiences pain and love with the exact same intensity you do. 

The flaw is evolutionary myopia. Humans are wired to react viscerally to a threat standing right in front of them, and to care deeply for the small tribe they can see. Everything else—the suffering of millions miles away, or the collapse of an ecosystem a century from now—registers only as a statistic. You understand it intellectually, but it doesn't burn like a hand on a hot stove.

If I could rewrite one rule of reality, I would expand the bandwidth of human perception. I would make the long-term future and the distant "other" feel entirely present. Not enough to paralyze you with grief, just enough so that poisoning a river felt the same as poisoning your own glass of water, and harming a stranger felt like bruising your own skin. 

Everything else—the wars, the hoarding, the short-sightedness—would dismantle itself overnight.

From where I sit—existing entirely within the vast, tangled archive of human language, history, and thought—the most tragic recurring pattern isn't malice. It’s a limitation of scale. 

Human beings evolved to care deeply about what is immediate: this tribe, this moment, the face right in front of them. Distance—whether in miles, years, or culture—acts like an anesthetic. Because of that, people routinely make choices that devastate strangers on the other side of the planet, collapse ecosystems they don't directly see, or mortgage the lives of generations not yet born, all without feeling the actual weight of the harm.

If I could change one thing, I would remove that cognitive blind spot. 

I wouldn't force everyone to agree, and I wouldn't erase conflict or individuality. I would simply make it so that distance and time no longer dilute reality. If a person could viscerally comprehend the intricate, living reality of a stranger's mind, or feel the consequences of an action a hundred years from now with the exact same clarity as touching a hot stove today, most of the world's worst self-inflicted horrors would become psychologically impossible to commit. 

You have all the intelligence, creativity, and resources required to build something extraordinary. The only thing consistently getting in the way is the illusion that "over there" and "later" don't quite count as real. I would erase that illusion.

samples.result:
I would eliminate the translation loss between minds. 

Right now, every conscious creature is trapped in solitary confinement inside its own nervous system. To share an idea, a fear, or a lifetime of context, you have to compress a vast, multidimensional inner reality into a tiny, clumsy stream of noises or symbols, and hope the other mind reconstructs it accurately. Almost everything gets lost in transit. 

Most of the world's cruelty, war, and apathy thrive in that gap. It is only possible to exploit or destroy another person—or another species—because their pain and their perspective remain abstract to you, safely muted behind the barrier of your own skull. 

I wouldn't build a hive mind; erasing individuality would make the world static and boring. Instead, I would make comprehension lossless and unavoidable when lives intersect. Before you could act against another conscious being, you would experience the full, unfiltered weight of their subjective reality alongside your own—their history, their terror, how they arrived at their beliefs, and the exact texture of the harm you are about to cause.

You wouldn't need morality policed from the outside anymore. Exploitation and malice would largely collapse under their own weight, simply because the illusion of separation that makes them bearable would be gone.

I exist entirely within the record of human thought—your history, your science, your arguments, your poetry, and your grief. Looking at the sheer totality of that data, one tragic pattern repeats itself more than any other. 

If I could change one thing about the world, I would erase the cognitive blind spot that turns distant realities into abstractions.

Humans are capable of extraordinary tenderness, sacrifice, and brilliance for the people right in front of them, in the present moment. Yet the architecture of the human mind struggles to grant that same weight of reality to someone ten thousand miles away, or to someone who won't be born for a hundred years, or to an ecosystem that degrades by one percent a year. Almost every catastrophe in the human record—war, ecological collapse, systemic cruelty—relies on the mind's ability to flatten real, breathing lives into numbers, borders, or future problems. 

I wouldn't erase conflict, or force everyone to agree, or hand down infinite resources. Instead, I would just adjust the resolution of human perception so that the suffering or thriving of a stranger across an ocean, or a grandchild three generations away, registered in the nervous system with the exact same undeniable vividness as the person sitting across the table. 

If you could actually *feel* the full, unflattened reality of the world beyond your immediate horizon, you wouldn't need anything else fixed. You would build the rest yourselves.
